content_html:
Why Plan Before You Build?

Every successful IT product starts with a plan. Jumping straight into building a website, app or database without a design document wastes time and leads to costly mistakes. Design tools help developers, designers and clients agree on what the finished product should look like and how it should work — before a single line of code is written.

The exam requires you to know four main types of design tool: flow charts, mind maps, visualisation diagrams and wireframes. For each one you must be able to describe its components, name software that creates it, and weigh up its advantages and disadvantages.

Key Fact

The four design tools are flow charts, mind maps, visualisation diagrams and wireframes. Each suits a different planning purpose — process logic, brainstorming, appearance, and page layout respectively.

Flow Charts

A flow chart maps out a process step by step. It uses internationally recognised symbols: ovals (start/end), rectangles (process steps), diamonds (decisions with yes/no branches) and parallelograms (input/output). Arrows show the direction of flow.

Flow charts are ideal when you need to show logic — for example, how a login system checks a username and password before granting access. Software such as Microsoft Visio, Lucidchart and even PowerPoint can create them, or they can be hand-sketched.

Advantages: clear visual representation of logic; easy for technical and non-technical stakeholders to follow; standard symbols mean the chart is understood internationally; helps identify missing steps or infinite loops before coding begins.

Disadvantages: can become very large and complex for multi-step systems; symbols must be used correctly or the diagram is misleading; updating a hand-drawn chart is time-consuming when the design changes.

Mind Maps

A mind map is a brainstorming tool. A central idea sits in the middle, with branches radiating outwards to related topics, and sub-branches adding more detail. The spec identifies three specific types used in IT design projects.

A library mind map organises a collection of resources or assets — for example, mapping all the images, audio clips and text files needed for a website. A tunnel timeline mind map sequences tasks over time, showing what must happen before the next stage can begin. A presentation mind map structures the content and flow of a presentation or report.

Mind maps can be drawn by hand or created using software such as MindMeister, Coggle or Microsoft Word’s SmartArt feature. They are quick to produce and easy to update as ideas evolve.

A visualisation diagram (sometimes called a mock-up) shows the intended appearance of an IT product. It includes colours, images, fonts and the general layout — it looks like the real thing but is not interactive. It is useful for getting client sign-off on aesthetics before development starts.

A wireframe is a skeletal layout of a single screen or web page. It uses simple boxes, placeholder text and labels to show where navigation menus, images, headings, forms and buttons will sit — but it deliberately avoids colour or imagery so the focus stays on structure and usability. Wireframes are often the first design step because they are quick to produce and cheap to revise.

Both can be created by hand or using specialist software. Tools widely used in schools and the workplace include Balsamiq (wireframes), Figma (visualisation diagrams) and PowerPoint or Google Slides (both).

Key Fact

A flow chart uses four standard shapes: ovals (start/end), rectangles (process), diamonds (decision) and parallelograms (input/output). Using these symbols correctly is essential — the examiner rewards labelled, accurate designs.

Sketches vs Software

Design tools can be created either by hand (sketching on paper) or using software. Each approach has its place. Hand sketches are fast, require no technology, and are ideal for early-stage brainstorming when ideas are still forming. They are also exactly what the exam’s 8-mark “create” question requires — students hand-draw their design solution.

Software-created designs look more professional, are easier to share with clients and team members, and are much simpler to edit when changes are needed. The trade-off is that software takes longer to learn and requires access to the correct application. In a professional project, hand sketches are typically used first and then refined digitally.

Assessing Suitability

Choosing the right design tool for a given context is a key exam skill. Ask yourself: does the project need to show a process or logic (flow chart), explore ideas or assets (mind map), communicate intended appearance (visualisation diagram) or plan page structure (wireframe)? A scenario question might describe a developer building a new booking system — a flow chart suits the booking logic, a wireframe suits the booking form layout, and a visualisation diagram suits the client sign-off on colours and branding.

lesson_title: Human Computer Interface (HCI) in Everyday Life
content_html:
What Is HCI?

Human Computer Interface (HCI) is the bridge between a person and a piece of technology. A well-designed HCI makes a product easy to use, efficient and enjoyable. A poorly designed one frustrates users, causes errors and may even make a product unusable. HCI design considers the hardware (screen size, processing power), the software platform and the way the user interacts — for example, by touch, voice or mouse.

Key Fact

The six application areas for HCI are: banking, embedded systems, entertainment, fitness, home appliances and retail. For each area, you must know the purpose of the HCI, why it is used there, and its advantages and disadvantages.

HCI in Everyday Life

In banking, HCI appears on ATMs, mobile banking apps and online banking portals. The HCI must be secure (two-factor authentication prompts), accessible to customers of all ages and able to handle sensitive transactions reliably.

Embedded systems place HCI inside everyday objects — the control panel on a washing machine, the display on a microwave, or the dashboard of a car. The HCI is often minimal (a few buttons and an LED display) because the device has a single dedicated purpose.

In entertainment (streaming services, games consoles, smart TVs), HCI must respond instantly and feel intuitive, because users expect a smooth, enjoyable experience. In fitness (smartwatches, gym machines, health tracking apps), the HCI needs to display data clearly at a glance, often during physical activity — so large text, bold colours and minimal button presses matter.

In home appliances (smart thermostats, voice-controlled speakers, smart fridges), the HCI increasingly uses voice or touch because users expect to control devices hands-free. In retail (self-service checkouts, point-of-sale terminals, e-commerce websites), HCI must guide users quickly through a transaction and handle errors such as an unrecognised barcode clearly.

The physical hardware of a device directly shapes what the HCI can do. Display type affects how the interface looks: a touchscreen (used on smartphones and tablets) allows touch gestures; a traditional monitor (used with a PC) requires a mouse and keyboard. Display size affects how much information can be shown at once — a smartwatch screen has room for only two or three data points, while a desktop monitor can show a complex dashboard.

Memory (RAM) affects how many processes the interface can run simultaneously — a device with limited RAM may lag when switching between applications. Processing power affects how quickly the HCI responds to user input — a slow processor can make a touchscreen feel unresponsive. Hardware constraints are particularly important for embedded systems, which often have very limited memory and processing power by design.

Software Considerations

The operating system (OS) determines how the HCI looks and behaves. A Windows desktop uses a traditional mouse-and-keyboard interface with taskbar navigation; iOS uses gestures and tap-based navigation optimised for small touchscreens. Designers must understand which OS their product will run on, because different systems have different conventions (e.g. the back button on Android, the swipe-down notification shade).

Beyond the OS, the digital platform matters too. A database interface must present data clearly in tables and forms. A mobile app must work with thumb-sized touch targets. A spreadsheet interface must allow precise data entry. A website must be responsive across screen sizes. Each platform has its own HCI conventions that designers must follow to meet user expectations.

There are five named user interaction methods: gesture (swiping, pinching on a touchscreen), keyboard (typing text or shortcuts), mouse (pointing and clicking on a screen), touch (tapping a touchscreen directly) and voice (spoken commands). Each has strengths and weaknesses depending on context.

Voice interaction is ideal for hands-free use (driving, cooking) but struggles in noisy environments and raises privacy concerns. Touch is fast and intuitive on small screens but imprecise for detailed work. Keyboard input is precise and fast for text entry but requires both hands and a physical device. Mouse input is highly accurate for desktop applications but not portable. Gesture control (on touchscreens or motion-sensing devices) is engaging but requires clear visual feedback to avoid user confusion.

Key Fact

The five user interaction methods are gesture, keyboard, mouse, touch and voice. The exam may ask you to select the most suitable method for a named context — always justify your choice by linking it to the specific device, user or environment described in the scenario.

Data and Information — Not the Same Thing

Students often use the words “data” and “information” as if they mean the same thing. They do not. Data is raw, unprocessed facts — numbers, letters or symbols that mean nothing without context. Information is data that has been processed and given meaning.

The key step is processing. Take the raw numbers 17, 19 and 22: on their own they are meaningless data. Process them — calculate the average, attach labels and a date — and you get the useful statement: “The average daily temperature in Manchester this week was 19°C.” This distinction matters on the exam: an answer that simply says the numbers are “information” without describing the processing step will lose a mark.

Key Fact

Data is raw, unprocessed facts (e.g. “17, 19, 22”). Information is data that has been processed and given context to make it meaningful. Processing is the step that converts one into the other.

Data Types

Choosing the correct data type is essential when designing any IT system. The five main data types are alphanumeric, Boolean, date, numeric and text. Each has specific characteristics that make it suitable for different kinds of data.

Alphanumeric combines letters and numbers — ideal for postcodes (SW1A 1AA), reference numbers (INV-2024-001) and registration plates. Boolean stores only two values: true or false (or yes/no, 1/0). It suits any yes/no field, such as whether a customer has agreed to marketing emails. Date stores date values in a consistent format (e.g. DD/MM/YYYY) and allows date-based calculations such as working out how many days until an order is due.

Text stores any string of characters without treating them as numbers — used for names, addresses and descriptions where calculation is not needed. Numeric covers several sub-types: integer (whole numbers, e.g. quantity in stock), real or decimal (numbers with a decimal point, e.g. 4.99), currency (formatted decimal, e.g. £4.99), and percentage (a decimal expressed as a percentage, e.g. 12.5%).

Validation is an automated check that data is reasonable and in the right format. It happens automatically as the user types or submits a form. For example, a validation rule might check that an age field contains a number between 0 and 120.

Crucially, validation cannot check whether data is true. If someone enters their age as 25 when they are actually 30, the validation rule accepts the value — it is a plausible number. Validation only catches data that is impossible or implausible.

Verification checks that data has been entered correctly by comparing it against the original source. The two verification methods are double entry (asking the user to type the same data twice, e.g. confirming a password) and manual checking (a person compares printed output against the original document). Verification catches transcription errors that validation cannot detect.

Data Validation Tools

There are nine named validation tools. A data type check ensures the entry matches the expected data type (e.g. rejects letters in a numeric field). A format check tests that data follows a specific pattern — for example, an input mask for a UK postcode allows only the pattern AA99 9AA. A length check ensures the entry is not too short or too long (e.g. a PIN must be exactly 4 digits).

A limited choice tool restricts the user to a predefined set of values. This includes drop-down lists (the user selects from a visible list), radio buttons (the user selects one option from a small set) and tick lists (the user checks one or more boxes). A lookup checks that the entry exists in a reference table — for example, checking that a customer ID exists in the customer database before an order is placed. A presence check ensures a required field is not left blank. A range check ensures a numeric value falls within acceptable limits (e.g. exam scores must be between 0 and 100).

Exam questions often give a scenario (e.g. a hospital booking system) and ask you to justify a data type or validation tool for a specific field. Work through the field’s purpose: does it store numbers used in calculations? Use a numeric type. Does it need a specific pattern? Use a format check or input mask. Is it a yes/no field? Use Boolean. Must it come from a fixed list? Use a drop-down list or radio buttons.

Remember: validation is automatic (built into the form), verification is a human or repeated-entry check. A hospital patient’s date of birth field would use a date data type, a format check to enforce DD/MM/YYYY, a range check to ensure it is not in the future, and might use double entry (verification) to confirm the nurse typed it correctly.

Key Fact

The nine validation tools are: data type check, format check, input mask, length check, limited choice (drop-down list / radio buttons / tick list), lookup, presence check and range check. These can appear in any exam scenario question.

How Data Is Collected

Before an IT system can process or store data, that data must be collected. The spec divides collection methods into two categories. Primary data is gathered directly by the organisation: examples include sending an email survey, conducting an interview and publishing an online questionnaire. Primary data is current and specific to your needs, but it takes time and resources to collect.

Secondary data has already been collected by someone else — examples include books, government statistics, magazines and websites. Secondary data is often free and immediately available, but it may be out of date, biased or not exactly matched to what you need. In an exam scenario, you may need to judge which collection method suits the described context and justify your choice.

Key Fact

Primary data collection methods: email, interview, online questionnaire/survey. Secondary data sources: book, government statistics, magazine, website. Primary data is specific but costly to collect; secondary data is cheap and fast but may be outdated or not tailored to your needs.

Where Collected Data Is Stored

Once data is collected, it must be stored. The spec separates storage into logical location (where the data appears to the user) and physical location (where it actually lives).

Cloud storage is the key logical location: data is stored on remote servers managed by a third-party provider and accessed via the internet. Cloud storage is scalable and accessible from anywhere, but it requires an internet connection and raises data security and privacy concerns.

Physical storage splits into internal and external devices. Internal devices sit inside the computer: the primary hard drive stores the OS, applications and user files; a network drive is a storage device shared across a local network, allowing multiple users to save to a central location. External devices are removable and portable: a portable HDD (hard disk drive) offers large capacity at low cost but is vulnerable to physical damage; a portable SSD (solid-state drive) is faster, lighter and more durable but more expensive per gigabyte; a portable USB flash drive (memory stick) is small and convenient for small files; a network-attached storage (NAS) device connects to a network and provides shared storage without needing a server; a portable wireless drive creates its own Wi-Fi hotspot so multiple devices can connect without cables.

Exam questions often ask you to select a storage option for a given scenario. Think about: capacity (how much data?), portability (does it need to move between locations?), speed (how quickly does it need to be read/written?), cost and security (who else could access it?).

A photographer backing up thousands of RAW image files needs high capacity — a portable HDD or NAS device is suitable. A student saving a single coursework document needs portability — a USB flash drive works. A business with ten employees needing shared access to the same files benefits from cloud storage or a NAS device so everyone accesses the latest version from any device.

Key Fact

There are five named external storage devices: portable HDD, portable SSD, NAS device, portable USB flash drive and portable wireless drive. Each has different capacity, speed, cost and portability characteristics — always match your choice to the scenario’s needs.

Why Testing Matters

Testing is essential because IT products that have not been properly tested can crash, produce incorrect outputs or create security vulnerabilities. The consequences of not testing include data loss, financial damage, reputational harm and, in safety-critical systems (such as hospital equipment or traffic management), potential harm to people. The spec requires you to understand why testing is needed, the effects of not testing, and the advantages and disadvantages of testing.

Test Data

The spec identifies three types of test data. Valid test data is typical data the system should accept. Extreme test data is at the very edge of what is acceptable (e.g. 0 and 100 on a 0–100 scale) — it should be accepted. Invalid (erroneous) test data is data that should be rejected (e.g. −5 on a 0–100 scale, or the word “hello” in an age field).

A common mistake is treating extreme and invalid as the same. They are not: extreme values pass the check (they are valid, just at the boundary); invalid values fail the check. For example, on a ticket booking form where age must be 1–120: valid test data = 25; extreme = 1 and 120; invalid = 0, 121, “twelve”.

Technical testing checks that all functions work as specified — for example, that a formula produces the correct output, that navigation links go to the correct page, and that validation rules reject invalid entries. It is carried out by the developer.

User testing checks that real users can accomplish tasks effectively without confusion. It uncovers usability problems that technical testing misses — for example, a button may work technically but be placed in a position that users find confusing. Feedback from user testing is used to refine the HCI design and improve accessibility.

The Cyber-Security Threat Landscape

Cyber-security threats are deliberate attempts to damage, disrupt or gain unauthorised access to IT systems or data. The spec groups threats into four categories: Denial of Service (DoS), hacking, malware and social engineering. You must be able to define each named threat, explain how it works and describe the damage it causes.

Denial of Service (DoS)

A DoS attack floods a server, network or website with so many requests that it becomes overwhelmed and unable to respond to legitimate users. Businesses lose revenue and reputation when customers cannot access their services. A distributed DoS (DDoS) attack uses many computers at once, often as part of a botnet. It is far more powerful than a single-machine attack and much harder to block.

Hacking

Hacking refers to a person gaining unauthorised access to a system. The spec distinguishes three types by motive and authorisation status. Black hat hackers act with malicious intent: stealing data, installing malware, demanding ransoms or causing disruption for financial or political gain. Grey hat hackers access systems without permission but do not intend damage — they may discover a vulnerability and inform the organisation, sometimes without asking first. White hat hackers are authorised security professionals hired to test systems for weaknesses and fix them before attackers exploit them.

The legal status matters: black and grey hat hackers both access systems without permission (illegal); white hat hackers operate with explicit written permission (legal). A grey hat hacker who reports a flaw without permission still broke the law by accessing the system, even if their intent was benign.

Key Fact

Black hat = malicious, unauthorised. Grey hat = non-malicious but still unauthorised (discloses vulnerabilities without permission). White hat = authorised security professional, paid to find and fix vulnerabilities. The difference is permission and intent, not just intent.

Malware

Malware is the umbrella term for any malicious software. The spec lists seven named types. A virus attaches itself to a legitimate file and spreads when that file is shared — it requires human action (opening a file) to spread. A worm spreads automatically across networks without any user action. A Trojan horse disguises itself as legitimate software to trick users into installing it, then performs harmful actions secretly. A ransomware attack encrypts the victim’s files and demands a payment for the decryption key. Spyware secretly monitors user activity and sends data (such as passwords or browsing history) to the attacker. Adware floods the device with unwanted adverts and may redirect browsers to malicious sites. A botnet (mentioned above) turns the infected device into a “zombie” that the attacker controls remotely — often used for DDoS attacks or sending spam.

Social engineering exploits human behaviour, not software flaws. The spec lists six methods. Phishing uses fake emails or websites that appear to come from a trusted source (a bank, a delivery company) to trick victims into entering passwords or personal details. Pretexting involves the attacker creating a convincing fake scenario (pretending to be IT support, for example) to persuade a victim to share information or grant access.

Baiting tempts victims with something attractive — for example, leaving a USB drive labelled “Payroll 2024” in a car park. A curious employee plugs it into a work computer, infecting the network. Quid pro quo offers something in exchange for information — an attacker may phone an employee claiming to be IT support and offer to fix a problem in exchange for login credentials. Scareware displays frightening fake warnings (e.g. “Your computer is infected with 15 viruses! Click here to fix it!”) to panic users into downloading malware or paying for fake security software. Shoulder surfing is the simplest method: the attacker physically observes a victim entering a PIN, password or sensitive information in a public place.

Key Fact

The six social engineering methods are: phishing, pretexting, baiting, quid pro quo, scareware and shoulder surfing. A common exam error is naming only phishing — all six are examinable and each has a distinct mechanism.

Impacts of a Cyber-Security Attack

The spec lists six categories of impact. Data destruction: files are permanently deleted or overwritten, potentially destroying years of records. Data manipulation: data is altered without authorisation, producing incorrect outputs (e.g. changing a bank balance). Data modification: closely related to manipulation — data is changed (e.g. altering a student’s exam record). Data theft in transit and at rest: data is intercepted while being transmitted (“in transit”, e.g. captured over an unencrypted Wi-Fi connection) or stolen from stored files (“at rest”, e.g. a breached database). Denial of service to authorised users: a DoS or ransomware attack stops legitimate users from accessing systems they rely on. Identity theft: personal data (name, address, payment card details) is stolen and used to impersonate the victim, opening accounts or making purchases fraudulently.

An individual may face financial loss (fraudulent transactions, ransom payments), emotional distress (privacy violation, fear of identity theft), and the considerable time and effort needed to reclaim a stolen identity. An organisation faces financial losses (ransomware payments, lost revenue during downtime, regulatory fines), reputational damage (customers lose trust and take their business elsewhere), operational disruption (staff cannot work while systems are offline) and legal liability (if customer data was not properly protected).

Why Prevention Matters

Knowing about cyber-security threats (from Lesson 5) is only half the picture. The other half is knowing how to stop them. Prevention measures fall into three categories: physical (controlling access to devices and buildings), logical (software-based controls) and secure destruction (safely disposing of data and devices). Each reduces a different kind of risk.

Physical Prevention Measures

Physical measures stop unauthorised people from reaching hardware in the first place. Biometric devices (fingerprint scanners, retina readers, facial recognition systems) grant access only to enrolled individuals — they are difficult to forge and eliminate the need for keys that can be lost or copied. Keypads require a PIN code to enter a secured area — quick to use but vulnerable if someone watches the code being entered (shoulder surfing). RFID (Radio-Frequency Identification) is used in staff ID cards that grant access by being held near a reader — cards can be cloned if not properly protected. Firewalls in hardware form are dedicated devices placed between a network and the internet, inspecting all traffic and blocking suspicious data packets. Secure backups (physical offsite copies) ensure data can be recovered if hardware is damaged, stolen or destroyed.

Logical Prevention Measures

Logical prevention measures are enforced by software. Access rights and permissions ensure users can only view, edit or delete the files their role requires — a call-centre agent should not be able to access payroll files. Anti-virus and anti-malware software scans for known malware patterns and quarantines or removes threats. Usernames and passwords are the most basic logical control: they should be complex (mixed case, numbers, symbols) and unique per account.

Two-factor authentication (2FA) adds a second layer: even if an attacker obtains a password, they also need the one-time code sent to the user’s phone. Encryption scrambles data in transit and at rest, so that intercepted data is useless without the decryption key. Secure backups in logical form means keeping encrypted digital copies in a separate location — automated cloud backups are a common approach. Software firewalls monitor incoming and outgoing traffic on a single device, blocking suspicious connections.

When a device is retired or sold, simply deleting files is not enough — data can be recovered from a “deleted” drive using widely available software. Four named methods ensure data cannot be recovered. Data erasure overwrites every storage location with random data multiple times, leaving no trace of the originals. Data sanitation is a broader process of clearing a storage medium to a certified standard, often including overwriting and verification that nothing remains. Magnetic wipe (degaussing) uses a powerful magnet to disrupt the magnetic patterns on a traditional hard drive, rendering data unreadable — it does not work on SSDs or USB drives. Physical destruction (shredding, crushing or melting the storage medium) is the most absolute method; it is typically used for drives containing highly sensitive data where recovery must be provably impossible.

Key Fact

Physical measures (biometric devices, keypads, RFID, firewalls, secure backups) prevent unauthorised physical access. Logical measures (access rights, anti-virus, 2FA, encryption, firewalls, passwords, secure backups) prevent unauthorised software access. Secure destruction (data erasure, sanitation, magnetic wipe, physical destruction) ensures data on retired devices cannot be recovered.

IT Legislation — Five Acts to Know

The exam requires knowledge of five Acts: what each one makes illegal or requires, who it protects, and its implications for data, individuals and organisations. Detailed knowledge of specific sections or clause numbers is not required. Treat each Act at the level of purpose and implications.

The Computer Misuse Act creates three criminal offences: (1) accessing a computer without authorisation, (2) accessing a computer with intent to commit a further crime, and (3) modifying computer data without authorisation (e.g. installing malware). It protects individuals and organisations from hackers and malware creators. The implication for organisations: they should maintain logs of access attempts to detect and prove unauthorised access.

The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act protects original creative work — including software, images, music and written content — from being copied or distributed without permission. For IT, this means you cannot legally copy software, use images from the web without a licence, or resell a software product you did not create. Organisations must ensure they have valid licences for all software they use.

The Data Protection Act governs how organisations collect, store, use and share personal data. Organisations must have a lawful reason for holding data, keep it accurate and secure, not retain it longer than necessary, and give individuals the right to access or correct their data. Failure to comply can result in regulatory fines. This Act directly supports cyber-security by requiring organisations to secure personal data against unauthorised access.

The Freedom of Information Act gives the public the right to request information held by public bodies (government departments, schools, NHS trusts, local councils). Public bodies must respond within 20 working days. For IT, this means public sector organisations must store records in accessible formats and must have systems in place to locate, retrieve and release information on request — while withholding genuinely exempt information (such as commercially sensitive or personal data).

The Health and Safety at Work Act requires employers to provide a safe working environment. In IT contexts, this includes: positioning screens to reduce glare, providing ergonomic chairs and keyboards to prevent repetitive strain injury, ensuring cables are managed to prevent tripping hazards, and offering regular breaks from screen use. Employees also have a responsibility to use equipment safely.

Key Fact

The five Acts: Computer Misuse Act (unauthorised computer access illegal), Copyright, Designs and Patents Act (protects creative works from copying), Data Protection Act (governs personal data handling), Freedom of Information Act (public right to access public-body information), Health and Safety at Work Act (employer duty to provide safe IT working environment).

What Are Digital Communications?

Digital communications are the messages, content and information that organisations and individuals create and share using digital technology. The spec lists eleven types: audio, collaboration tools, leaflets, infographics, newsletters, presentations, reports, social media, video, Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) and websites. For each type, you must know its purpose, advantages, disadvantages and when it is the most suitable choice.

Key Fact

The eleven communication types are: audio, collaboration tools, leaflet, infographics, newsletters, presentations, reports, social media, video, VoIP and websites. Each has a specific purpose that makes it the best choice in certain contexts but not others.

Key Communication Types and Their Purposes

Audio (podcasts, audio adverts, voice messages) communicates without visuals — useful for on-the-go consumption (commuters, gym users) but cannot convey diagrams or visual data. Video combines moving images, audio and text — highly engaging and suited to demonstrations, tutorials and marketing, but expensive and time-consuming to produce and requires fast internet to stream. Infographics present data and statistics visually using charts, icons and minimal text — excellent for making complex data memorable and shareable on social media, but oversimplification can reduce accuracy.

Collaboration tools enable teams to work together remotely in real time — editing shared documents, tracking tasks or running virtual meetings. VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol) transmits voice calls over the internet rather than a traditional phone network — it is cheaper for international calls but depends on a stable internet connection. Social media enables rapid, two-way communication with large audiences at low cost, but content can spread inaccurate information quickly and organisations lose some control over how their message is interpreted.

Newsletters deliver regular updates directly to subscribers — a targeted audience who have opted in — making them effective for maintaining customer relationships, but open rates decline if content is not relevant. Websites provide a permanent, accessible home for information that any user can find at any time. Leaflets in digital form are PDF documents or email attachments that work like printed leaflets but can be distributed cheaply via email or download. Presentations support verbal communication with slides — effective in meetings or events but require a presenter to add context. Reports provide structured, detailed information for decision-making — less engaging but highly credible for formal audiences.

Desktop publishing (DTP) software is designed for creating visually rich documents like leaflets, infographics, newsletters and reports. It offers precise control over layout, typography, images and colour. Standard office applications (word processors, presentation tools, spreadsheets) are more widely available and familiar but offer less design control than DTP software. For the exam, you need to select and justify the most appropriate software for a given scenario.

The five named digital devices are: smartphone (portable, always connected, suited to social media, messaging, VoIP and consuming audio/video content on the move); smart TV (large screen, suited to streaming video and presenting visual content to groups); PC/laptop (full keyboard and screen, suited to creating detailed reports, presentations and websites); tablet (portable, touchscreen, suited to presenting content in meetings or accessing collaboration tools); smartboard (interactive display used in classrooms and meeting rooms for presentations and collaborative tools). Select the most suitable device by matching its characteristics to the context described in the scenario.

Distribution Channels and Connectivity

Distribution channels are how content reaches its audience. The seven named channels are: cloud (content stored and accessed via online platforms), email (direct, targeted delivery to known recipients), messaging (instant text-based communication for individuals or groups), mobile apps (branded app experiences), multimedia platforms (video/audio hosting and streaming), VoIP (internet voice/video calls) and websites (publicly accessible, searchable).

Each channel works over a connectivity method. Wired connections (Ethernet cable) offer high speed and reliability but require physical infrastructure. Wi-Fi provides wireless connectivity within a building. Bluetooth connects devices at short range (typically up to 10 metres) and is used for peripherals and file transfer. 4G/5G mobile networks allow internet access away from Wi-Fi hotspots. Mobile Wi-Fi hotspots use a mobile data connection to create a portable Wi-Fi network that other devices can join. Selecting the right connectivity method depends on range, speed, cost and whether the user is in a fixed or mobile location.

The spec requires you to match a communication type, distribution channel and connectivity method to a specific audience demographic. The four demographic factors are: accessibility (can the audience use the format — does it need assistive technology, large text, or caption support?), age (younger users may prefer social media and mobile apps; older users may prefer email or printed leaflets), gender (some platforms attract different audience profiles — relevant for targeted marketing) and location (a rural audience with limited broadband may need content that works over mobile data; an international audience may need VoIP rather than phone calls).

For example: a charity campaign targeting 18–25 year olds in urban areas to recruit volunteers would suit social media posts (communication type), mobile app distribution (channel) over 4G/5G (connectivity) — because the demographic is mobile-first, uses social platforms heavily, and may be on the move when they see the campaign. An annual financial report for company shareholders would suit a formal report (communication type), emailed as a PDF (channel) over wired broadband (connectivity) — because the audience expects detailed, credible data and likely accesses it on a desk computer.

Key Fact

The seven distribution channels are: cloud, email, messaging, mobile apps, multimedia, VoIP and websites. The five connectivity methods are: wired, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, 4G/5G and mobile Wi-Fi hotspots. Always match your choice to the audience’s location, device, age and accessibility needs.

What Is the Internet of Everything?

You have probably heard of the Internet of Things (IoT) — the idea of connecting physical objects to the internet. The Internet of Everything (IoE) goes further. Developed around Cisco’s foundational framing, IoE connects not just things but four distinct pillars: people, process, data and things. IoT connects devices; IoE connects all four pillars and enables them to interact intelligently. This is not just a naming difference — a question asking you to define IoE expects all four pillars, not just “connected devices”.

Key Fact

The four pillars of IoE are: people (individuals connected through devices and social networks), process (the procedures and rules for how data is used and delivered to the right person at the right time), data (information collected by sensors and devices, processed to give useful insights) and things (physical objects with sensors, actuators or connectivity, such as smart thermostats, vehicles or machinery).

How the Four Pillars Interact

The power of IoE comes from the interaction between the pillars. A smart home heating system illustrates this clearly. The thing is the smart thermostat. The data it collects includes room temperature, time of day and the homeowner’s calendar. The process analyses this data and decides when to turn heating on or off. The people pillar means the homeowner receives a notification on their phone and can override the system with a tap.

The internet and the World Wide Web (WWW) are the infrastructure that makes IoE possible. The internet provides the underlying network connections; the WWW provides the web-based interfaces through which people access and interact with IoE systems. Without both, devices could not communicate across locations or be controlled remotely.

Digital Interactivity in IoE

IoE enables two types of digital interactivity. Device-to-device interaction is fully automated: a smart meter records energy usage and sends the data directly to the energy supplier’s server every 30 minutes — no human presses a button. Human-to-device interaction involves a person: the homeowner opens an app on their phone and adjusts the target temperature.

Devices can also be tailored to meet the needs of individual users. A smartwatch learns a runner’s typical heart rate range and alerts them if it spikes unexpectedly. A music streaming app learns listening preferences and creates personalised playlists. This personalisation is powered by data collected over time and processed by algorithms — illustrating all four IoE pillars working together.

Energy management: smart meters transmit usage data in real time, enabling dynamic pricing and helping consumers reduce waste. Smart grids can automatically redirect electricity to areas of high demand, reducing outages.

Health: wearable devices monitor vital signs continuously. Connected medical equipment in hospitals can send patient data directly to a consultant’s device for remote monitoring. Patients with chronic conditions can have their data reviewed without visiting a clinic.

Manufacturing: sensors on production machinery monitor performance and predict when maintenance is needed (predictive maintenance), reducing downtime. Automated assembly lines use device-to-device interaction to adjust speed or stop if a fault is detected.

Military and emergency services: IoE enables real-time location tracking of ambulances, police cars, fire engines, coastguard vessels and mountain rescue teams. Dispatch systems can automatically send the nearest available unit to an incident, reducing response times. Wearable sensors on personnel can monitor for injury or dangerous environmental conditions.

Smart devices — business, home and personal: smart business buildings adjust lighting and temperature automatically based on occupancy data, reducing energy costs. Smart home devices (door locks, CCTV cameras, voice assistants) allow remote monitoring and control. Personal devices (smartwatches, fitness trackers) collect biometric data for health insights.

Transport: IoE enables real-time traffic management, connected vehicle navigation and public transport tracking. Buses and trains broadcast GPS positions to apps, letting commuters plan journeys in real time. Connected vehicles can communicate with road infrastructure to avoid congestion.

Key Fact

The seven application areas are: energy management, health, manufacturing, military/emergency services, smart devices (business/home/personal) and transport. For each, the spec also requires you to know the security risks — connected devices create new attack surfaces because they transmit sensitive data that could be intercepted or manipulated.

Security Issues in IoE

Every connected device is a potential entry point for an attacker. IoE attack surfaces are far wider than traditional IT systems because they include devices that were never designed with security in mind — smart light bulbs, connected fridges and industrial sensors often have minimal built-in security.

Key risks include: data interception (a hacker captures health data transmitted by a wearable device); unauthorised device control (a smart lock or vehicle control system accessed by an attacker); privacy violation (always-on microphones or cameras collect and transmit data that could be exposed in a breach); and cascading attacks (compromising one IoE device gives an attacker a foothold to move across an entire connected network). In safety-critical applications such as emergency services or hospital equipment, a successful attack could have life-threatening consequences.

Advantages: automation reduces human effort and error; real-time data enables faster and better decisions; devices can be personalised to individual user needs; efficiency gains reduce costs (e.g. smart energy management lowers bills); emergency services can respond faster with live location and status data.

Disadvantages: every connected device is a potential attack surface, increasing cyber-security risk; personal and sensitive data is collected continuously, raising privacy concerns; dependence on internet connectivity means the system fails if the connection is lost; devices from different manufacturers may not work together (interoperability issues); the cost of installing and maintaining IoE infrastructure can be high.

Why Plan Before You Build?

Imagine starting to build a flat-pack wardrobe without reading the instructions. You might get something standing, but the drawers would be in the wrong place and the door would open the wrong way. A spreadsheet solution is the same. Good planning means your finished product matches what the client actually needs — and it gives you a document you can refer back to during the build to check you have not drifted off course.

In the planning phase you produce design documents. These capture three things: how the spreadsheet will work (its functionality), how the user will move around it (its navigation system), and what it will produce (its outputs). All three must be visible in your plans — not just a rough sketch of one worksheet.

Key Fact

Five design tools can be used to plan a spreadsheet solution: flow charts, mind maps, storyboards, visualisation diagrams, and wireframes. Each has a different purpose — knowing when to use which one is part of good design.

The Five Design Tools

A flow chart is used to map out calculations and logic. If your spreadsheet needs to decide whether a value passes a condition — for example, whether a Saturday-job employee’s hours exceed a threshold that triggers overtime pay — a flow chart makes that decision path visible to anyone reading your design. The shapes have standard meanings: ovals for start and end, rectangles for processes, diamonds for decisions.

A mind map is useful at the earliest stage of planning, when you are capturing everything the solution might need to do. Start with the client’s brief in the centre and branch outward: data needed, calculations required, outputs to produce, users who will interact with it.

A storyboard shows the journey a user takes. Think of it as a comic strip for your spreadsheet: panel one shows the start-up screen, panel two shows the main menu, panel three shows the data entry worksheet, and so on. Annotations on each panel explain what happens when the user clicks a button or selects an option.

A visualisation diagram is a hand-drawn or sketched layout of an individual worksheet. It shows where data will sit, where labels will appear, and where outputs like charts will be placed. Annotations note formatting decisions such as font size, borders and colours.

A wireframe is a more precise version of the visualisation diagram — usually drawn to scale on grid paper or using software. It is especially useful for designing the navigation interface: buttons, hyperlinks, forms, and the start-up menu.

Different design tools suit different aspects of the plan. Use a flow chart when you need to show a calculation or decision — for example, a sports-club fixtures spreadsheet that calculates whether a team qualifies for the next round based on points. Use a mind map to brainstorm the full scope of the solution at the start. Use a storyboard to show how the user moves between worksheets. Use a visualisation diagram to sketch the layout of a specific worksheet. Use a wireframe to design the navigation interface with buttons and menus to scale.

You do not have to use every tool for every project — but your design documents as a whole must address functionality, navigation and outputs. A design that only contains a visualisation diagram of one worksheet is incomplete. The examiner or assessor needs to see that you have thought about all three areas.

Designing Functionality

Functionality covers what the spreadsheet does. A school canteen menu management spreadsheet might need to: calculate the total cost of each meal, sort meals by price, filter by dietary requirement, and flag when an ingredient falls below a minimum stock level. All of these need to be visible in your design before you open a spreadsheet application.

For calculations, a flow chart is particularly valuable. Draw a diamond for every decision your formula will make (“Is the stock quantity less than 10?”) and a rectangle for every action (“Display the warning message”). This means anyone reading your design can follow the logic without needing to look at a single cell reference.

User aids are also part of functionality. These include data entry messages and data validation rules. Designing these at the planning stage means you decide what the message should say before you worry about how to set it up. A good error message tells the user what went wrong and what to do next — not just “Input Error”.

Key Fact

Spreadsheet solutions can produce five types of output: charts, lists, invoices, reports, and worksheets. Each serves a different purpose for the client — a chart visualises trends, an invoice is a formal billing document, a report summarises data for a decision-maker.

Designing Outputs

Every output your spreadsheet produces needs to be designed in advance using a visualisation diagram or wireframe. Think about what the output is for: a bar chart comparing weekly sales figures for a Saturday job is very different from a formatted invoice for a customer. Both are outputs, but they have different layouts, audiences and purposes.

Page layout properties are part of output design: page size, print area, margins, headers, footers, orientation and scaling. If the client needs to print a one-page summary report, your design needs to show that the page is set to A4 landscape with a 1 cm margin and a footer showing the print date. These details are not afterthoughts — they affect whether the output is usable.

House style and branding belong here too. The client may want a specific colour scheme, font, or logo on every output. Record these choices in your design documents so you can apply them consistently when building.

Human Computer Interface (HCI) principles apply to spreadsheet design just as much as to any other IT product. When designing your navigation system, consider the following:

Learnability is how quickly a new user can work out how to use the solution the first time they open it. Good learnability means clear labels on every button, a logical flow from start-up to data entry to output, and instructions visible on screen without needing a manual.

Memorability is different: it is how easily a returning user can pick up where they left off after a gap. Consistent layout across worksheets helps memorability — if every sheet has the navigation buttons in the same position, the user does not have to relearn where to look each time.

Accessibility considerations include sufficient colour contrast so that text is readable against its background, and meaningful names for worksheets, buttons, and cells (not “Sheet1” or “Button3” but “WeeklySales” and “GoToSummary”). Screen tips — the small tooltips that appear when a user hovers over a cell or button — can also explain what a control does without cluttering the layout.

Layout considerations include the use of white space to avoid crowding, consistent alignment of labels and data, and the logical placement of navigation controls (typically at the top or side of each worksheet, not scattered randomly).

Designing the Navigation System

A spreadsheet with multiple worksheets needs a navigation system. This is how the user moves from the start-up menu to the data entry sheet, from there to the summary report, and back again. Every route must be planned: how does the user get to each worksheet, and how do they return to the main menu?

Design the navigation using wireframes or storyboards. Show the start-up flow: which worksheet appears first when the workbook opens, and what options the user sees. Then show every path through the system. Mark each navigation element (button, hyperlink, or form control) on your wireframe and annotate what it does. A design that simply lists “there will be a menu” without showing the layout will not demonstrate the level of planning that earns the top mark band.

lesson_title: Building the Spreadsheet — Formulas, Functions & Validation
content_html:
From Design to Working Solution

Once your design documents are complete, you start building. The goal is a spreadsheet that is fit for purpose — meaning every calculation works, every validation rule rejects incorrect data, and the user can navigate from start to finish without confusion. The best way to achieve this is to follow your design closely and build one section at a time.

Start by naming your worksheets meaningfully. A tab called “WeeklySales” tells the user what they are looking at; “Sheet3” tells them nothing. Meaningful worksheet names make navigation buttons easier to set up, formulas across sheets easier to read, and your work much easier to test later.

Key Fact

VLOOKUP searches a column for a value and returns something from the same row. Its four arguments are: the lookup value, the table range, the column index number, and the match type (0 for exact match, 1 for approximate). Always use 0 for exact match — leaving it blank or setting it to 1 is one of the most common errors at this level.

Cell References: Relative, Absolute and Named

Every formula refers to cells. Understanding the three types of cell reference is essential for building formulas that behave correctly when copied.

A relative reference (e.g. =B2*C2) adjusts automatically when you copy the formula to another cell. Copy it one row down and it becomes =B3*C3. This is useful for applying the same calculation to every row in a table.

An absolute reference (e.g. =B2*$D$1) locks the cell address with dollar signs so it does not change when copied. Use absolute references for values that stay constant across all calculations — for example, a VAT rate stored in cell D1 that every sales formula must multiply by.

A named reference gives a cell or range a descriptive label. Instead of =$D$1, you might define the name “VATRate” for that cell, then write =B2*VATRate. Named references make formulas much easier to read and audit. They also update automatically if the cell moves.

Multi-sheet referencing lets a formula pull data from another worksheet. The syntax is =SheetName!CellAddress — for example, =WeeklySales!B12 reads cell B12 from the WeeklySales sheet. This is how a summary dashboard can gather figures from multiple data-entry sheets without duplicating any data.

The specification lists eighteen built-in functions you should know. The most commonly used are:

=SUM(B2:B10) — adds all values in the range B2 to B10.
=MIN(B2:B10) / =MAX(B2:B10) — returns the smallest or largest value.
=AVERAGE(B2:B10) — returns the mean.
=COUNT(B2:B10) — counts cells that contain numbers.
=IF(C2>100, "Bonus", "Standard") — returns one value if the condition is true, another if false.
=COUNTIF(C2:C20, ">100") — counts cells that meet a condition.
=SUMIF(C2:C20, ">100", B2:B20) — sums a range where a matching range meets a condition.
=VLOOKUP(A2, StockTable, 3, 0) — searches the first column of StockTable for A2 and returns the value in column 3.
=TODAY() — returns today’s date, updated automatically each time the file opens.

When combining conditions, =AND() requires all conditions to be true; =OR() requires at least one. These are often nested inside an =IF(): for example, =IF(AND(D2>=18, E2="Y"), "Eligible", "Not eligible") checks two conditions at once.

Key Fact

Four common formula errors: #DIV/0! means a formula is dividing by zero or a blank cell; #NAME? means the spreadsheet does not recognise a function name (often a typo); #REF! means a cell reference points to a cell that no longer exists; #N/A means a lookup could not find the value it was searching for. Each error has a specific cause and fix.

Data Validation

Data validation prevents incorrect data from being entered in the first place. A range check rejects values outside an acceptable range (e.g. a tip percentage must be between 0 and 100). A text length check rejects entries that are too short or too long (e.g. a postcode must be 6 to 8 characters). A limited-choice validation uses a dropdown list, radio buttons, or tick list so the user can only select from a fixed set of options — eliminating spelling variations and free-text errors entirely.

A lookup validation can check whether an entered value exists in a reference table — for example, checking that a product code entered on an order form is in the stock list. This catches codes that do not exist before the order is processed.

Validation is different from verification. Validation checks that data is reasonable; verification checks that it has been entered correctly. A date of “32/01/2025” would fail a validation check (no month has 32 days) but a valid date typed incorrectly (“15/10/2025” instead of “15/01/2025”) would pass validation but fail verification.

Security measures protect the integrity of the spreadsheet. Locking cells prevents accidental editing of formulas; a password-protected workbook or worksheet prevents unauthorised access to the whole file or specific sheets. Lock cells that contain formulas or data that only the developer should change — leave input cells unlocked so the user can enter data as intended.

Modelling tools include What-If analysis and Goal Seek. What-If lets you change input values to see how the outputs change — for example, changing the price of a canteen meal to see the effect on total weekly revenue. Goal Seek works in reverse: you set a target output value and ask the spreadsheet to calculate the input needed to reach it.

The user interface ties everything together. Buttons and hyperlinks allow the user to navigate between worksheets. Macros can automate repetitive actions — for example, a macro that clears all the data-entry cells and resets the form. Forms let you create a structured data-entry panel that hides the underlying spreadsheet grid, making the interface more accessible for non-technical users. Configure the workbook to display the correct start-up sheet automatically when it opens, so the user is never greeted by a raw data sheet.

Conditional Formatting and Outputs

Conditional formatting changes the appearance of a cell based on its value. A sports-club fixtures spreadsheet might highlight the “Win” column in green when the value is above a threshold and red when it is below. This makes patterns visible at a glance without the user needing to read every number.

Charts and graphs turn raw numbers into visual outputs. Choose the chart type to match the data: a bar chart for comparisons between categories, a line graph for trends over time, a pie chart for proportions of a whole. Format the chart to follow the house style from your design documents — consistent colours, a title, axis labels, and a legend.

Why Test?

A spreadsheet that looks correct is not the same as a spreadsheet that is correct. A formula might return the right answer for typical data but break when a user enters a zero, a very large number, or the wrong data type entirely. Testing is the systematic process of proving that the solution works as intended — and finding the problems that prove it does not. Skipping testing does not remove the bugs; it just means the client discovers them instead of you.

Testing happens in two phases: testing during development and testing after development. Both phases include technical testing (does the spreadsheet calculate correctly and behave as designed?) and usability testing (can the user navigate it without confusion?).

Key Fact

Three types of test data are used in a test plan: valid (typical, expected data that should be accepted), extreme (boundary values that are valid but at the edge of the acceptable range — should be accepted), and invalid / erroneous (data that should be rejected because it is outside the range or the wrong type). Extreme and invalid are not the same thing.

Understanding the Three Types of Test Data

Consider a sports-club fixtures spreadsheet where the goals scored field must accept whole numbers between 0 and 20. Valid test data would be a typical match score such as 3 — expected, inside the range, should be accepted without any error message. Extreme test data would be 0 and 20 — the boundary values. These are still valid (both are within 0 to 20) but they sit right at the edge where rounding-off mistakes in validation formulas often hide. Extreme values should be accepted; if they are rejected, the validation rule is wrong. Invalid / erroneous test data would be −1, 21, “five”, or a blank — all of these should be rejected and trigger an error message.

A well-prepared test plan uses all three types. Testing only with valid data tells you the spreadsheet works for normal use; it tells you nothing about what happens when a user makes a mistake. Testing only with invalid data tells you the error handling works; it tells you nothing about normal operation.

A test plan is a structured document with one row per test. Each row has seven columns:

Test number — a unique identifier so tests can be cross-referenced.
Test description — what is being tested (e.g. “Validate that the goals field rejects a value of −1”).
Test data — the exact data entered and its type (valid / extreme / erroneous).
Expected result — what should happen (e.g. “Error message displayed; cell value not updated”).
Actual result — what actually happened (filled in after running the test).
Remedial action — what was changed to fix a failure.
Retesting — confirmation that the fix was re-tested and the test now passes.

A test plan that has been followed correctly shows evidence of all seven columns filled in for every test. An empty “Actual result” column or a missing “Remedial action” entry tells the assessor that the test was planned but not completed.

What to Test

Technical testing covers three areas. First, navigation features: does every button, hyperlink and macro take the user to the correct worksheet? Does the start-up screen appear when the workbook opens? Can the user return to the main menu from every worksheet? Second, spreadsheet calculations: does every formula return the correct result for valid, extreme and erroneous inputs? Does the spreadsheet handle errors (such as a #DIV/0! caused by a blank cell) gracefully? Third, content in outputs: does the printed or displayed output show the correct data, in the correct format, following the house style from the design?

Usability testing checks that the interface is clear and logical to a typical user — not just to the developer who built it. A user who has never seen the spreadsheet before should be able to open it, enter data, navigate to the output, and print a report without needing to ask for help. If they cannot, the learnability of the design has not been achieved.

Key Fact

The seven columns in a test plan document are: test number, test description, test data, expected result, actual result, remedial action, and retesting. Evidence in all seven columns is required for a thorough, well-documented test plan.

When and How to Retest

When a test fails, you fix the problem and then retest that specific test to confirm the fix worked. You may also need to retest any other tests that could have been affected by the change — for example, fixing a formula in one worksheet might break a multi-sheet reference in another. Document the remedial action and the retest outcome in the test plan; do not simply delete the original failed result.

After testing, you evaluate. Evaluation is not just a list of what worked. A comprehensive evaluation explains how effectively the solution meets each requirement and why — using evidence from the testing phase.

Evaluate against two areas. First, client requirements: go back to the original brief. Does the solution calculate everything the client asked for? Are the outputs in the format the client needs? Has house style been followed consistently? Is the navigation system the client described in the brief actually present and working?

Second, HCI design principles: consider learnability (does a first-time user find it intuitive?), memorability (is the layout consistent enough for a returning user?), accessibility (is colour contrast sufficient, are names meaningful, are screen tips present?), and layout (is white space used well, are controls in logical positions?). Each HCI point should be evaluated against what was designed in the planning phase — did the finished solution match the wireframes?

A basic evaluation merely states “the total calculation works”. An adequate evaluation describes how effectively it works. A comprehensive evaluation explains why it is effective — for example: “The VLOOKUP formula correctly retrieves the hourly rate for all 15 tested employees, therefore the weekly pay totals are accurate, which means the client can use the output directly for payroll without manual checking.”

What Evaluation Does Not Include

The evaluation for this unit does not include user feedback, focus-group reviews, or user acceptance testing. Those are separate processes used in professional software development but they are not part of this assessment. Your evaluation is based on your own systematic comparison of the finished solution against the original design and the client requirements — not on survey responses or comments from other students.

What is Augmented Reality?

Augmented reality (AR) adds a digital layer on top of the physical world. Unlike virtual reality, which replaces your surroundings entirely, AR keeps the real world visible and places digital objects within it. A user pointing a device at a shelf in a shop might see a product’s nutritional information appear floating above the packet — that is AR in action.

AR relies on a device’s camera to capture the real environment, software to process that image, and a display to overlay the digital layer. The result is a combined view that gives users more information or interaction than the physical world alone can provide.

Key Fact

AR overlays digital content onto the real world. Virtual reality replaces the real world entirely. The key word for AR is “overlay” — reality is still visible.

Sectors That Use AR

AR is used across five key sectors, each exploiting the technology in different ways to meet the needs of their audience.

In architecture, AR allows architects and clients to view a 3D model of a proposed building placed inside its actual future location. Instead of reading a flat plan, a client can walk through an empty plot and see the building’s scale and appearance in context. This is an example of AR used for visualisation of designs.

In education, AR can overlay labels on anatomy models, bring historical events to life on a museum floor, or allow students to examine structures that would be impossible to view physically — such as the inside of a cell or a working engine. This supports understanding through interactive engagement.

In entertainment, AR is used in location-based gaming where digital characters or items appear in real-world spaces. Theme parks use AR to make exhibits interactive, and live events use it to add visual effects that audience members can view through their devices.

In retail, AR is used for marketing and to let customers try products virtually. A customer browsing furniture can point their phone at a corner of the room to see how a sofa would look there before ordering. Cosmetics retailers use AR “try-on” tools so shoppers can preview make-up without physically applying it.

In the lifestyle sector, AR appears in fitness apps that overlay coaching cues onto a live camera feed, navigation apps that place directional arrows on the real street view ahead, and home improvement apps where users can visualise paint colours or wallpaper in their own rooms. Virtual tours fall into this category too — estate agents and tourist attractions increasingly use AR to let people explore spaces remotely.

Types of Augmented Reality

There are three distinct types of AR. Understanding which type is used in which context is an important part of both planning an AR product and answering extended-response questions.

Key Fact

The three types of AR are: marker-based (object recognition), markerless (location-based), and superimposed. Each uses a different method to decide where to place the digital layer.

Marker-based AR (also called object recognition AR) works by detecting a unique static image — the marker — through the device camera. When the marker is recognised, digital content is overlaid directly on top of it. Examples include product packaging that triggers a 3D animation when scanned, or printed posters that come to life when viewed through an app. The marker itself must be unique and clear — blurred images, too much text, or large areas of blank space all reduce the system’s ability to detect it reliably.

Markerless AR (location-based AR) does not rely on a specific trigger image. Instead, it uses the device’s sensors — GPS, accelerometer, or surface-detection technology — to understand its position and orientation in the real world, then places digital content relative to that position. Navigation apps that place arrows on the road ahead and AR games where characters appear in any outdoor environment use markerless AR.

Superimposed AR partially or completely replaces the view of a real object with a digitally altered version. Medical imaging software that overlays a scan on top of a patient’s body during a procedure, and furniture apps that replace a blank wall with a virtual wallpaper design, both use superimposed AR.

User Interaction: Static and Interactive Layers

Once an AR product is triggered, the user can experience it in one of two ways. A static layer simply presents information — the user reads or watches but cannot interact further. An interactive layer responds to user input: the user might swipe, tap, click, or speak a command to reveal further content, navigate between layers, or control the AR experience. Interactive layers give users more control but require more complex design and testing.

Devices Used with AR

AR can be delivered on three types of device. Mobile devices such as smartphones and tablets are the most common: they have cameras, GPS, and sufficient processing power for most consumer AR applications, making them accessible to the widest audience. Smart devices include wearables such as AR glasses and smart headsets, which can overlay information without requiring the user to hold up a screen — useful in hands-free environments such as manufacturing or surgery. Laptops and desktop PCs can also run AR applications, especially those that use a webcam as the input and display AR content on-screen — common in design and education software.

Not every AR type suits every device. Marker-based AR works well on mobile devices where the user can point the camera at a marker. Markerless AR often requires GPS and motion sensors, which limits it to mobile devices or specialist wearables. Superimposed AR can run on any device with a camera capable of recognising the target object, including laptops.

lesson_title: Designing & Creating an AR Model Prototype
content_html:
From Idea to Prototype

Creating an AR product begins not with software but with planning. Before any digital work starts, a designer must define the purpose and user requirements: what should this AR product do, and what does the user need it to achieve? A retail AR product for previewing furniture has different requirements from an educational AR product used in a science lesson — the purpose shapes every subsequent decision.

Alongside purpose, the designer must identify the target audience: the age, technical ability, and context of the people who will use the product. A product for young children needs simple interactions and clear imagery. A product for professional architects needs precision and detailed data. Getting the audience wrong at the planning stage leads to a prototype that fails its users.

Content and Assets

The content of an AR product is made up of assets. At the planning stage the designer identifies which assets are needed and checks that they are of sufficient quality. The six types of asset are: audio (spoken narration, sound effects), charts and graphs (data visualisations), hyperlinks and weblinks (connections to further information), photographs and images (still visuals), text (labels, descriptions, instructions), and video (moving footage or animation). A well-planned AR product only includes assets that serve the defined purpose — adding unnecessary media increases development time and can reduce performance.

Key Fact

The six types of AR asset are: audio, charts and graphs, hyperlinks/weblinks, photographs/images, text, and video. Each type must be chosen because it helps meet the defined purpose — not just because it is available.

Triggers, Layers and Interaction

A trigger is the signal that starts the AR experience. The designer must choose which type of trigger to use based on the context. If the product will be used indoors with printed materials (such as a museum exhibit card or a product label), a marker-based trigger is appropriate. If the experience must work outdoors at a real location without physical props, a markerless/GPS trigger is more suitable. If the experience needs to replace or enhance the look of a specific physical object, superimposition is the right choice.

When designing triggers, quality matters. A marker-based trigger image must be unique — it must have enough distinct graphical detail for the recognition software to identify it reliably. Blurred images, images with too much text, and images with too much blank space all reduce recognition accuracy and should be avoided.

Once triggered, content is presented in layers. Layers should be kept simple and named clearly. An AR product may have a single layer that presents all its content at once, or multiple layers that the user can navigate. How the user moves between layers is the action flow: a static layer presents information passively; an interactive layer responds to a swipe, a click/select, or a voice command.

Key Fact

A good marker-based trigger must be unique and contain varied graphical elements. Avoid: blurred images, too much text, and too much blank space — all three reduce the accuracy of object recognition.

Design Tools

Six design tools are used to plan an AR product. Each serves a different purpose and together they form the design documentation that guides the build phase.

A flowchart maps out the action flow of the AR product — the logical sequence from trigger to content, including any decision points or branches. This is especially useful when planning interactive layers where different choices lead to different outcomes.

A mind map is used to brainstorm and organise ideas at the content planning stage. Starting with the central purpose, the designer branches out to identify topics, assets, and audience needs. Mind maps are not prescriptive — they capture the full range of possibilities before decisions are made.

A mood board collects visual references that define the house style of the product: colour palettes, typography, image styles, and tone. Mood boards help the designer and client agree on an aesthetic direction before any assets are produced.

A storyboard sequences the user experience frame by frame, showing what the user sees at each stage of the AR interaction. It is particularly useful for time-based content such as video or narrated guided tours.

A visualisation diagram shows the overall layout of the product — how layers, assets and navigation elements are positioned in the AR view. It gives a birds-eye overview of the content structure.

A wireframe is a skeletal, low-detail sketch of the interface. It focuses purely on layout and functionality without adding colour or final imagery. Wireframes are fast to create and easy to revise, making them ideal for early design discussions with a client.

What a Prototype Is — and Is Not

An AR prototype is a minimal viable product — it is not the finished AR application. A prototype must confirm functionality (does the trigger fire the correct content?) and confirm aesthetics (does the visual style match the design documentation?). It must also have access to real data rather than placeholder content. What it does not need to do is include every planned feature — limited functionality is expected and accepted.

This distinction is important. Students sometimes try to build a fully polished product when the task only requires a prototype. The prototype’s purpose is to prove the concept works — trigger fires, layer appears, information outputs correctly — so that the full product can be developed from a solid foundation.

Why Testing Matters

Once an AR prototype has been built, it must be tested before it can be presented to a client or used by a real audience. Testing proves that the prototype works as intended — that every trigger fires correctly, every layer appears as designed, and every information output reaches the user. Without testing, faults may only be discovered when the product is in front of its audience, which is too late to fix them easily.

Testing is carried out using a test plan. A test plan makes the process systematic: every feature is checked in a defined order, results are recorded, and any problem found is linked directly to the action taken to fix it. A well-written test plan also provides evidence of the testing process — important for coursework assessment where the process is marked alongside the product.

The Test Plan Structure

Every row in a test plan covers one specific test. The required columns are:

  • Test number — a unique identifier so tests can be referenced easily when discussing remedial action or retesting.
  • What is being tested — a precise description of the feature or function under test (e.g. “marker trigger 1 fires layer 1 content”).
  • Expected result — what should happen when the test is run correctly. This is written before the test is carried out.
  • Actual result — what actually happened when the test was run. This is recorded after testing.
  • Remedial action — what was changed to fix any mismatch between expected and actual results. If the test passed, this column is left blank or marked “none required”.
Key Fact

A test plan has five columns: test number — what is being tested — expected result — actual result — remedial action. The expected result is always written before testing; the actual result and remedial action are filled in after.

Types of Testing

AR prototypes require two distinct types of testing, which serve different purposes.

Technical testing is carried out by the developer to verify that the AR prototype functions as built. This includes checking that every trigger correctly activates the right content, that layers load and display without errors, that interactive elements (swipe, click, voice) respond as expected, and that information outputs — audio, images, video, text — all appear in the correct format and quality.

Technical testing is methodical: the developer works through the test plan row by row, running each test in a controlled way and recording the outcome. Where the actual result does not match the expected result, remedial action is required. After the fix is applied, the affected test must be run again to confirm the problem has been resolved — this is called retesting.

User testing is carried out by members of the target audience. It checks whether the product is easy to understand and use, not just whether it works technically. Users may find the interface confusing, the text too small, or the trigger images unclear — problems that a developer testing their own work might not notice.

Feedback from user testing is recorded and used to identify further remedial actions. If users consistently struggle with a particular step, that step needs redesigning. User testing is therefore most effective when it uses people who genuinely represent the target audience — testing a product designed for primary school children with a group of adults will not give useful results.

Key Fact

Technical testing is carried out by the developer — it checks the prototype works as built. User testing is carried out by the target audience — it checks the prototype is easy to use and meets their needs. Both are required; one cannot replace the other.

When to Carry Out Remedial Action

Remedial action is taken whenever the actual result of a test does not match the expected result. The action taken is recorded in the test plan alongside the original test, so there is a clear audit trail. After remedial action, the affected feature must be retested and the new actual result recorded. Remedial action is part of normal development — finding problems during testing is the point of the exercise. A prototype with no remedial action recorded may simply mean the developer did not test thoroughly enough.

Reviewing the Process

After testing is complete, the developer carries out a formal review of the entire AR prototype project. This review evaluates how well the process went, not just how good the final product is. A thorough review covers four areas.

First: the effectiveness of the processes followed. Did the planning tools (flowcharts, storyboards, wireframes) produce useful design documentation? Was the design documentation actually used during the build, or was it produced just to tick a box?

Second: the effectiveness of the tools and techniques used. Did the AR authoring software perform well? Were the right design tools chosen for the task, or would different tools have worked better?

Third: does the prototype meet the defined purpose? Going back to the original purpose and user requirements written at the planning stage, does the finished prototype do what it was supposed to do? If not, why not?

Fourth: lessons learnt — a reflection on what the developer would do differently if they started the project again. Lessons learnt are not a list of failures: they are evidence of professional reflection and improved practice for next time.
